title: Reading Gaits: What the Trail Tells You
summary: A single track names the animal; the PATTERN of tracks names what it was doing — and often narrows the species faster than the print itself.

sections.heading: Four gaits to know
sections.body: Walk — slow, alternating steps in two near-parallel lines. Trot — a faster two-beat gait; many animals "register" the hind into the front track, collapsing the trail into one tidy line. Bound — front feet land, then the hinds swing past and land ahead, leaving clusters (weasels, squirrels). Gallop / lope — top speed; all four feet group, then a long gap, with the larger hind feet printing AHEAD of the fronts.

sections.heading: Direct register = a wild tell
sections.body: When the hind foot drops exactly into the front print, you get a single clean line of evenly spaced tracks. Foxes, coyotes and cats do this constantly — it is efficient and quiet. A pet dog rarely bothers: its trail wanders and double-prints. A dead-straight line of single prints leans wild; a sloppy side-to-side trail leans domestic dog.

sections.heading: Measure stride, straddle, group
sections.body: Stride is the distance to the next same-foot print — it scales with leg length and speed. Straddle is the width of the whole trail — wide means a low, heavy body (raccoon, badger), narrow means a tidy walker (fox, cat). Group length in a bounder hints at size and speed. These survive even when an individual print is mushy.

sections.heading: Let the pattern break the tie
sections.body: When two species leave near-identical prints (fox vs small coyote, dog vs coyote), the gait pattern usually decides it: purposeful straight trotting line vs meandering wander. Always read 6–10 prints of trail before committing to the single print under your nose.

title: Track vs. Sign: The Two Halves of Tracking
summary: A footprint is only half the story. Scat, feathers, chews, rubs and beds often identify an animal when no clean track exists.

sections.heading: What counts as "sign"
sections.body: Sign is anything an animal leaves besides a footprint: scat (droppings), feathers and fur, chews (gnawed nuts, browsed twigs, gnawed wood), rubs and scrapes (antler rubs, bear trees, scent scrapes), diggings, beds, and trails worn into vegetation. In hard or leaf-littered ground where tracks won’t form, sign is often all you get — and it can be more diagnostic than a smudged print.

sections.heading: Read track and sign together
sections.body: The strongest IDs combine both: a clawless round track PLUS a covered, hair-filled scat says cat. A long-fingered "hand" track PLUS a streamside latrine says raccoon. When the track is ambiguous, the nearby sign frequently resolves it.

sections.heading: Leave it as you found it
sections.body: Photograph sign in place with something for scale; don’t collect or disturb. Fresh scat, in particular, is data — note its contents and condition, then move on.

title: Scat ID Basics: Shape, Size, Contents, Place
summary: Droppings are one of the most reliable signs. Four questions narrow them fast — without touching anything.

sections.heading: Shape & ends
sections.body: Tubular cords with tapered or twisted points → carnivores (fox, coyote, cat, mustelids). Pellets → herbivores (deer, hare, rabbit). A clumped mass of pellets → pig or sometimes deer in rich forage. A long thin scat with a fine point → a mustelid like marten.

sections.heading: Contents
sections.body: Hair and bone → a meat eater. Berry seeds and insect parts → an omnivore (fox, raccoon, bear in season). Fish scales with a fishy smell → otter. Chalky white when dry → high bone content, classically hyena. Coarse fibre → a browser/grazer.

sections.heading: Size scales with the animal
sections.body: Diameter is a better size cue than length. A 2–4 cm thick cord is wolf or big dog; ~1 cm is fox; pellet size separates hare from deer from moose. Always note a measurement.

sections.heading: Place is a clue
sections.body: Latrines on logs/rocks → raccoon or otter. Prominent trail junctions and rocks → canids and cats scent-marking. Dung pits near a sett → badger. In water → beaver/muskrat. Where it’s left is part of the ID.

title: How Fresh Is It? Aging a Track
summary: You can’t put an exact clock on a print, but edges, weather and debris give a reliable rough age.

sections.heading: Read the edges
sections.body: Crisp, sharp rims with fine detail and moist-looking soil = fresh, often within hours. Crumbling, rounded, dried-out edges = a day or more. Wind slowly softens everything, so sharpness fades with time.

sections.heading: Use the weather as a timestamp
sections.body: Did it rain or snow last night? A track ON TOP of fresh snow or un-rain-pocked is younger than the last precipitation; a track filled with rain dimples or dusted by snow is older. Dew, frost and a known last-rain time are your free clock.

sections.heading: Debris and traffic
sections.body: Wind-blown leaves, twigs or insect trails crossing the print accumulate with age. Overlapping later tracks (other animals, your own) also order events. In snow, refreezing turns a fresh soft edge into a hard glazed one overnight.

sections.heading: Stay honest
sections.body: Aging is a range, not a number. "A few hours" or "more than a day" is the right level of confidence — anyone who gives you an exact time from a photo is guessing.

title: Reading the Substrate: Mud, Sand, Snow & Dust
summary: The same foot prints differently in different ground. Knowing the surface stops you from over- or under-reading a track.

sections.heading: Mud & wet sand — the truth-tellers
sections.body: Fine damp mud and wet sand capture the most detail: pad shape, claw dots, even fur and skin texture. This is where to confirm a tricky ID. Very wet mud, though, lets toes splay and prints slump larger than life.

sections.heading: Snow — size lies
sections.body: Snow exaggerates. Sun and melt widen a print over hours, so a "wolf" track may be a melted-out coyote. In powder, foot fur blurs pads (fox, lynx, hare) — read the gait and trail line instead of toe detail, and measure soon after the snow fell.

sections.heading: Dry sand & dust — shape only
sections.body: Loose dry sand collapses fine detail; you get overall shape and depth but not pad lobes or claw dots. Look for the cleanest print in the set and use the trail pattern to back up the ID.

sections.heading: Always note the surface
sections.body: Record what the animal walked on alongside the measurement. A 3-inch print in slumped mud and a 3-inch print in firm dust are not the same animal — context corrects the number.
